stories.title: Registry tier filter — one shared entrypoint accepts --tier {fast,medium,daily}, partitioning by expected_update_interval_seconds with no row dropped or duplicated
stories.description:
As the owner, I want one shared pipeline entrypoint that can be told which cadence tier to
collect, so a future fix to fetch/write/heartbeat logic needs one change instead of three
duplicated scripts, and so no registry row can silently fall through a filter gap or land in
two tiers at once.

The registry's `expected_update_interval_seconds` field already exists and already discriminates
exactly three values across all 71 entries (verified at G1: `300` x12, `28800` x4, `86400` x55).
This story adds the filter; it does not change what any indicator's cadence is declared to be.

# PRD-012 · Split cadence — research

## What we already knew, and whether it still holds

| Claim from our knowledge base | Still true? | What the source says | Citation |
|---|---|---|---|
| GitHub Actions `schedule:` runners are the compute layer (owner decision 2026-09-08, measured reachability) | **Holds** | Not contradicted by anything found. Reachability was measured for spot/derivatives/on-chain venues, not a cadence question. | (internal, `10-architecture.md`) |
| "GH Actions cron is documented to delay and occasionally drop runs" (already flagged as residual risk in the architecture doc) | **Holds, and is worse than the architecture doc implies for sub-hourly cadence** | GitHub's own docs: "The `schedule` event can be delayed during periods of high loads... High load times include the start of every hour... some queued jobs may be dropped." Independent measurement: "About 1 in 10 lands 5+ minutes late. About 1 in 50 lands 15+ minutes late," with community reports of 60+ minute delays at peak. | https://docs.github.com/en/actions/using-workflows/events-that-trigger-workflows#schedule , https://crontap.com/blog/github-actions-cron-drift-problem |
| "cron-job.org, already used elsewhere in this project's stack" as a fallback trigger mechanism | **Holds as a viable alternative, needs one correction** | cron-job.org supports down to 1-minute intervals on the free plan ("no rate limiting on 1-minute intervals") but is explicit that punctuality is *not guaranteed*: "delay time before running cronjobs ranging from 4 to 40 seconds." It is a better floor than GH Actions' 5-minute minimum + peak-hour drift, but it is not a hard real-time guarantee either — the freshness bound still needs slack for this. | https://cron-job.org/en/faq/ |
| Healthchecks.io free tier (20 checks) is "the single highest value-per-effort defence" | **Holds, and directly supports a per-tier design** | Healthchecks.io's own docs recommend one check per monitored job ("you would create a separate check for each cron job to be monitored") with a Grace Time set "a little above the expected duration of your cron job" — i.e. the product already has headroom (contract-canary uses one dedicated check today; PRD-012 would add at most 1–2 more, well inside the 20-check free tier). | https://healthchecks.io/docs/configuring_checks/ |
| "each job is a separate CI runner with a separate IP" (brief's stated risk about splitting collection multiplying vendor rate-limit exposure) | **Partially wrong — the premise doesn't hold on GitHub-hosted runners** | GitHub-hosted runners are ephemeral VMs with pool egress; "each job is an ephemeral VM... you'll almost certainly see two different addresses" even for *runs of the same workflow*. This is already true today for the single `ingest` job — every run already gets a fresh IP within Azure/Azure US ranges. Splitting into fast/medium/daily jobs does not introduce a *new* multi-IP exposure; that exposure already exists per-run. What splitting *does* change is call-volume clustering in time, not apparent source diversity. | https://docs.ipconfig.io/guides/github-actions-runner-ip , https://github.com/orgs/community/discussions/26884 |
| "The existing `contract-canary` workflow... does not need to be rebuilt" | Not independently web-verifiable (internal artifact) — confirmed by reading `.github/workflows/canary.yml` directly rather than the web; no correction needed here. | — | (file read, not web) |

## Existing implementations

No public reference implementation matches this exact shape (multi-tier crypto-indicator collection split across GitHub Actions cron tiers with a separate contract-canary heartbeat), but the individual pieces are each well-trodden:

- **GitHub Actions as a scheduler for data pipelines** is a widely-documented pattern, but every serious writeup converges on the same caveat this PRD must design around: treat `schedule:` "as a trigger source, not the clock" for anything time-sensitive, and prefer running the real clock in an external scheduler (cron-job.org, EventBridge, etc.) that fires `workflow_dispatch`/`repository_dispatch` — GitHub Actions supplies compute, not punctuality. https://crontap.com/blog/github-actions-cron-drift-problem
- **cron-job.org + `repository_dispatch`** is exactly the pattern this repo's own architecture doc already committed to as the "independent second trigger" for `ingest` — this PRD's fast tier is a natural extension of an already-adopted pattern, not a new integration.
- **Healthchecks.io "one check per job" with per-check Grace Time** is the vendor's own documented best practice for exactly this problem (multiple independently-scheduled jobs each needing their own dead-man's-switch): https://healthchecks.io/docs/configuring_checks/

## Approach options

**Option A — Three separate GitHub Actions workflows (fast/medium/daily), each with its own `cron:` and its own `HEALTHCHECKS_PING_URL_*`**
How it works: split `ingest.yml` into `ingest-fast.yml` (`*/5 * * * *`, the 12 five-minute OKX rows), `ingest-medium.yml` (8-hour cron, the 4 funding-rate rows), and `ingest-daily.yml` (renamed current job, the 54 daily rows). Each filters the registry by its own tier at runtime (`expected_update_interval_seconds` already exists as the discriminator — no new registry field needed).
Trade-offs: Simplest to reason about; reuses the exact `expected_update_interval_seconds` field the registry already carries. But the fast tier inherits GitHub's documented 5-minute-minimum + peak-hour drift risk (https://docs.github.com/en/actions/using-workflows/events-that-trigger-workflows#schedule) — a run landing 15 minutes late against a 600s freshness-warn bound (`btc_open_interest` etc.) means the cell reads `WARN`/`STALE` through no fault of the vendor or the code, purely GH Actions queue congestion at top-of-hour.
Cost: $0 (same GH Actions free-tier minutes budget, just redistributed across three workflows instead of one — total call volume is unchanged, only its clustering).
Who uses it: This is the "just use GH Actions schedule directly" default seen across most GH-Actions-as-cron writeups; it's the cheapest to build and matches what `sol-active-addresses.yml` already precedent-sets (dedicated workflow per tier).

**Option B — Same three-tier split, but the fast tier is triggered by cron-job.org → `repository_dispatch` instead of native GH Actions `schedule:`**
How it works: identical job bodies to Option A, but `ingest-fast.yml` drops its `schedule:` trigger entirely and listens only for `repository_dispatch` (type e.g. `ingest-fast`); a cron-job.org job fires that dispatch every 5 minutes.
Trade-offs: Removes GH Actions' documented top-of-hour congestion risk for the tier that actually can't absorb a 15-minute miss (600s/450s freshness bounds). Costs one more moving part (a cron-job.org job to configure and monitor) but the project's architecture doc already adopted cron-job.org as the fallback trigger for exactly this reason. cron-job.org itself is not zero-drift either (4–40s dispatch delay, https://cron-job.org/en/faq/) but that is two orders of magnitude tighter than GH Actions' reported 5–30+ minute peak drift.
Cost: $0 (cron-job.org free tier).
Who uses it: This is precisely the pattern the crontap writeup recommends for any schedule tighter than hourly (https://crontap.com/blog/github-actions-cron-drift-problem), and matches this project's own architecture-doc precedent of cron-job.org as "an independent second trigger."

**Option C — Keep one combined job, add a `--tier` flag, and just tighten the single cron to run more often**
How it works: don't split workflows; instead call the existing `ingest` entrypoint every 5 minutes but have it internally skip any indicator whose `expected_update_interval_seconds` hasn't elapsed since its last write (idempotent no-op for daily/medium rows most runs).
Trade-offs: Avoids multiplying workflow files, but every run — even the ~283 out of 288 daily runs per day that do nothing — still pays the fixed CI overhead (checkout, `uv` setup, DB connection) for zero benefit, and a single job now has to reason about mixed timeout budgets (the fast tier's OKX calls plus a daily row's occasional TA-Lib recompute in the same process). This directly risks recreating the known "a live fetch that fits its API budget can still break a scheduled job on wall-clock time alone" failure mode already logged against this exact codebase — a slow daily-tier fetch inside a job now running every 5 minutes shrinks the effective timeout budget for the fast tier sharing that same run.
Cost: $0, but wastes the most GH Actions minutes of the three options (288 daily invocations vs. Option A/B's daily job running once).
Who uses it: Not found in any external writeup for exactly this reason — the "one flexible cron, skip internally" pattern is a known anti-pattern once tiers diverge by more than ~10x in frequency, which this registry's 300s vs 86400s split (288x) clearly does.

**Recommendation: Option B.** The 5-minute tier's own freshness contract (450s stale bound) cannot absorb GH Actions' own documented delay behavior at that cadence, and the project has already adopted cron-job.org as a trigger mechanism for exactly this reason — Option B is a small, already-precedented extension, not new infrastructure. The 8-hour and daily tiers can stay on native GH Actions `schedule:` (Option A) since a 15–30 minute drift is immaterial against a 43200s/108000s freshness bound.

## Edge cases and gotchas

- **The wall-clock-vs-rate-limit distinction already bit this exact codebase once** (Helius/Solana fetch measured against credit budget but not against the CI job's own 10-minute timeout, taking 2.5h against a 10-minute limit). The current `ingest.yml` has `timeout-minutes: 10` (confirmed by reading the file). Splitting into a 5-minute-cadence fast-tier job means that job's *own* wall-clock budget must be far under 5 minutes end-to-end (checkout + `uv` install + 12 OKX calls + writes), or successive scheduled runs will start overlapping/queueing — verify this with a real timed run, not an estimate, exactly as the prior incident's fix note prescribes.
- **OKX's public market-data rate limit is per-IP, not per-account**, and open-interest specifically is rate-limited at roughly 20 requests per 2 seconds (community-sourced, OKX's own per-endpoint doc page did not resolve the number directly on fetch — flagging this as **UNVERIFIED at the primary-source level**, sourced instead from a secondary aggregator). At 12 five-minute-tier rows × one call each, this PRD's fast tier is nowhere near that ceiling even before considering that GitHub-hosted runner IPs are already ephemeral per-run (see table above) — so the brief's stated worry about "multiplying rate limits across separate runner IPs" does not hold on the numbers found; the real constraint is wall-clock timeout, not rate limit.
- **GH Actions top-of-hour congestion is not evenly distributed** — delays cluster specifically "at the start of every hour" per GitHub's own docs. A fast-tier cron of `*/5 * * * *` hits every hour-boundary by construction, so if the medium/daily tiers are *also* scheduled near `:00`, all three tiers' worst-case-drift moments coincide. Stagger daily/medium cron minutes away from `:00`/`:05` (GitHub's own recommendation: "schedule your workflow to run at a different time of the hour," https://docs.github.com/en/actions/using-workflows/events-that-trigger-workflows#schedule) — the existing `ingest.yml` already does this (`cron: '17 */6 * * *'`, offset 17 minutes), so this practice just needs to be preserved, not newly invented, when the workflow is split.
- **A public repo's scheduled workflow auto-disables after 60 days of no repository activity** (GitHub's own docs, confirmed above) — worth noting for whichever new workflow file is least likely to see commits touching it, though this repo is presumably private and this is likely moot; **UNVERIFIED** whether the repo is public or private from research alone.

## Services and keys this PRD needs

| Service | Why | Env var | Already provisioned? |
|---|---|---|---|
| cron-job.org | External trigger for the 5-minute fast tier, if Option B is chosen, to avoid GH Actions' documented schedule drift at sub-hourly cadence | none (webhook target is a GitHub `repository_dispatch` endpoint using a PAT) | Likely yes — architecture doc states cron-job.org is "already used elsewhere in this project's stack"; confirm which existing workflow uses it and reuse its dispatch token rather than minting a new one |
| Healthchecks.io | One additional check + Grace Time for the fast-tier job's own heartbeat, separate from `HEALTHCHECK_URL_CONTRACT_CANARY` and the existing daily-ingest heartbeat | e.g. `HEALTHCHECK_URL_INGEST_FAST` | Not yet — new check needed, but well within the 20-check free tier |

## Open questions for the human

| Question | My hypothesis | What breaks if I'm wrong |
|---|---|---|
| Is Option B (cron-job.org-triggered fast tier) worth the extra moving part, or is Option A (native GH Actions cron, accept the drift) good enough given the fast tier is "only" OKX derivatives, not a user-facing price feed? | **B** — the freshness contract (450s stale) is tight enough that GH Actions' own documented 5–30min peak drift would produce false-STALE reads often enough to be noisy, and the infra (cron-job.org) already exists in this stack. | If A is chosen and I'm right, expect recurring false-STALE alerts on the fast tier around top-of-hour, indistinguishable from a real vendor outage — increases on-call noise for the one-person team this product serves. |
| Does the registry's `expected_update_interval_seconds` field already cleanly partition into exactly 3 tiers with no in-between values, or are there rows at other intervals not shown in the brief's table? | I derived the 3-tier split (300/28800/86400, excluding the already-separate weekly SOL row) from a spot-check of `registry.yaml`; the brief's table matches what I read. | If a 4th interval value exists uncounted, a workflow built around exactly 3 files would silently drop that row into the wrong tier or no tier at all — worth a full `grep -c expected_update_interval_seconds` pass before the spec is written, not assumed from the brief. |
| Should the fast-tier job share the same Python entrypoint/module as the daily job (with a `--tier fast` filter argument), or be a genuinely separate script? | Shared entrypoint, tier as a CLI/env filter — avoids duplicating fetch/write/heartbeat logic across three files for what is fundamentally the same pipeline running on different rows. | If tiers diverge into separate scripts, a fix to shared logic (e.g. a corroboration-tolerance bug) now needs three coordinated PRs instead of one, reintroducing exactly the kind of duplication PRD-002's determinism harness was built to prevent. |

## Blind spots

1. **The brief's own stated worry (rate-limit multiplication across runner IPs) is the wrong risk, and the real risk it's gesturing at — wall-clock timeout collision under a tightened cadence — is the one that has *already caused a production incident in this exact codebase* (the Helius 2.5h-vs-10min timeout). Nobody has yet stated a wall-clock budget for the *new* fast-tier job specifically; without a real timed dry run, the same class of bug (works in isolated testing, breaks against the scheduler's actual clock) is one dry-run away from recurring.**
2. **Splitting `ingest.yml` into three workflow files without splitting `contract-canary.yml`'s vendor list means a canary shape-check can pass while a fast-tier write job silently fails** (e.g. wrong tier filter drops a row from every fast-tier run) — the canary checks endpoint *shape*, not that the correct *set* of rows was actually written by the correct job on the correct cadence. The adversarial case in the brief (force a fast-tier cell stale) tests exactly this, but only if someone remembers to also test "does the daily job's tier filter now silently swallow a row it shouldn't."
3. **No one has checked whether OKX's rate limit counts *scheduled polling cadence itself* as abusive** (bot-detection / ToS interpretation) separately from the raw requests-per-second ceiling — a 5-minute-cadence automated poll running indefinitely is a very different traffic pattern from ad-hoc human API usage, and OKX's API Agreement (https://www.okx.com/en-us/help/okx-api-agreement) was not read in depth during this research; **UNVERIFIED** whether continuous 5-minute automated polling of public endpoints violates any usage-pattern term distinct from the numeric rate limit.

## Sources

# 10 · Technical architecture

Derived from `research/R0`–`R7`. Where this document conflicts with a single research track,
`R7-cross-track-synthesis.md` explains why — the tracks could not see each other.

Retained as fallback only |

## The compute decision — CLOSED by measurement, 2026-09-08

> **Measured, not assumed.** GitHub Actions run `34199227365`, `ubuntu-latest`, egress
> Moses Lake US (Azure AS8075). Evidence committed at
> `prds/PRD-001-spine/50-evidence/US-011/reachability-ci.json`.
>
> | Venue | From US runner | From Beirut |

> | OKX | **200** | 200 |
> | Coinbase | **200** | 200 |
> | Kraken | **200** | 200 |
> | Coin Metrics | **200** | 200 |
> | alternative.me | **200** | 200 |
> | Binance spot | **451** | 200 |
> | Binance futures | **451** | 200 |
> | Bybit | **403** | 200 |
>
> **Decision: GitHub-hosted runners.** OKX — chosen by R3 on data-quality grounds as the only
> venue that flags a closed candle — is reachable, so the primary spot source and the free
> runner are compatible. **No self-hosted runner, therefore no resident process to supervise,
> therefore the prior system's failure mode cannot recur.**
>
> **Consequence for PRD-004 (derivatives):** Binance *and* Bybit are both blocked from US
> compute. Derivatives must come from **OKX**, or that PRD alone must run on non-US compute.
> R7 §C1 flagged this as unresolved; it is now resolved, and it is a genuine constraint
> discovered weeks before it would otherwise have surfaced.
>
> The tripwire in `20-decisions.yaml` fired exactly as written — a 451 appeared — but on
> venues the design had already moved away from, which is the outcome the design was chosen
> for rather than a lucky escape.

The reasoning that produced this question, retained because it explains the shape of the
architecture. Full version in `R7 §C1`.

The prior system's worst outage traces back through a chain that starts with a data-source
choice:

```
Binance chosen as primary source
  -> Binance returns HTTP 451 to US IPs
    -> GitHub-hosted runners (US) unusable
      -> self-hosted runner on Fly.io Frankfurt
        -> a long-lived process the owner must supervise
          -> exited 0 on self-update, stopped silently
            -> 24h of data lost before anyone noticed
```

The prior repo states this in its own workflow file: `# runs-on self-hosted because Binance is
unreachable from GitHub-hosted runners;` with `primary_region = 'fra'`.

**R3 independently recommends Coinbase/Kraken as primary spot OHLCV with OKX as cross-check**
— on data-quality grounds, because OKX is the only venue found that explicitly flags a closed
candle. That recommendation, taken up, dissolves the chain above: no Binance, no 451, no
self-hosted runner, no silent-death failure mode.

**Derivatives were the open remainder, and the spike settled them too.** Binance dominates
funding/OI/liquidations, and whether OKX and Bybit geo-block *unauthenticated public
market-data endpoints by IP* — as opposed to restricting US *accounts*, a different thing
routinely conflated — could not be established from Lebanon, where everything responds.
Measured from the runner: **Bybit returns 403 and Binance 451, while OKX returns 200.**
Derivatives therefore come from OKX, or PRD-004 runs on non-US compute.

**PRD-001 began with a reachability spike** (US-011, formerly US-001) that runs on the real target compute
and records, per venue and endpoint, the observed HTTP status. That table now exists and the
compute row above is decided. The two shapes it chose between were:

| | If venues are reachable from GitHub-hosted runners | If they are not |
|---|---|---|
| Trigger | GitHub Actions `schedule:` at off-peak minutes + cron-job.org `repository_dispatch` as an independent second trigger | Same |
| Compute | The GitHub-hosted runner itself | A **stateless** Fly.io machine in `fra`, started per run via the Machines API and stopped on exit — never resident |
| Residual risk | GH Actions cron is documented to delay and occasionally drop runs silently | Machine start failures — caught by the same dead-man's-switch |

Both shapes keep the dead-man's-switch and neither reinstates a supervised long-lived process.

---

## What "live" means here

**Provably fresh, not streaming.** Verified cadences of the actual sources (R7 §C2):

| Source | Genuine cadence |
|---|---|
| Spot OHLCV | seconds–minutes |
| Funding rate | 8h fixed (Binance); 1h–8h *dynamic* (OKX/Bybit) |
| On-chain (Coin Metrics) | one point per UTC day |
| Fear & Greed | daily |
| M2 | monthly, 3–4 week release lag |

Exactly one row moves faster than eight hours. A push layer would deliver real-time updates
for **price alone** while every other panel sat unchanged for hours — and the prior system
already measured the cost of that choice: a resident WebSocket listener starved the scheduled
jobs and was reverted (R0/F10).

So the browser **polls** (TanStack Query, 30–60s). The product's value is that a stale number
announces itself, not that a fresh one arrives in 50ms. *The repository name invites the
opposite assumption and should not be allowed to drive the design.*

---

## Cadence — collection and liveness are separate concerns

Decided 2026-09-09 after measuring what the sources actually publish.

**Almost everything on this board changes once a day or slower.** BTC's daily close, Coin
Metrics on-chain, and Fear & Greed produce one value per UTC day; ETF flows one per weekday at
T+1; M2 one per month, and it arrives 69 days late (measured). Only funding moves faster, at
three settlements a day.

So a 6-hourly *data* run fetches an identical value three times out of four. That is waste.

But cadence is not really about freshness — it is about **how long a failure stays invisible**.
A once-daily pipeline that breaks is undetectable for 24h plus grace, which is precisely the
blind spot that cost the prior system a full day of signals. Slowing collection to match the
data would optimise the thing that does not matter and worsen the thing that does.

**Therefore two jobs, not one:**

| Job | Cadence | Does | Cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| **collect** | **once daily**, shortly after 00:00 UTC when daily closes settle | fetches every indicator, writes datapoints, pings the heartbeat | ~2 min |
| **canary** | **every 6h** | pings each source's cheapest endpoint and the heartbeat. Writes **no** datapoints | ~20 s |

The canary makes failure visible in ~6–8h while collection stays honest at daily. It also
catches a source outage *before* the daily run needs it — you learn at 06:00 that OKX is
unreachable, instead of finding a hole at midnight.

Roughly 120 GitHub Actions minutes a month against a 2,000 limit.

**The owner is only interrupted when something is wrong**: the heartbeat's failure endpoint on
an errored run, and Healthchecks' DOWN alert on silence. A healthy day sends nothing.

Freshness budgets follow from this, not the other way round: an indicator's `freshness_warn`
and `freshness_stale` are derived from **its own** publication interval, so a daily series is
not marked stale merely because the page was opened in the afternoon.

## Shape

```
                    TRIGGER (redundant, independent)
   GitHub Actions schedule:  ──┐        ┌── cron-job.org -> repository_dispatch
                               ▼        ▼
                      ┌──────────────────────────┐
                      │   INGEST (Python 3.12)   │
                      │                          │
                      │  registry.yaml  ← the single source of truth:
                      │    per indicator: vendor, endpoint, FIELD,
                      │    freshness budget, definable-for-assets
                      │            │             │
                      │            ▼             │
                      │  fetchers ── return Ok | Stale | Unavailable | Error
                      │            │    (never a bare float)
                      │            ▼             │
                      │  compute (TA-Lib, pure: f(bars, window))
                      │            │             │
                      │            ▼             │
                      │  integrity checks ── coverage generated FROM registry
                      └────────────┬─────────────┘
                                   │  ping on success
                                   ├──────────────► Healthchecks.io ── alerts on SILENCE
                                   ▼
                      ┌──────────────────────────┐
                      │  SUPABASE POSTGRES       │
                      │  datapoints (long/narrow)│
                      │   value, status,         │
                      │   source_vendor, endpoint│
                      │   fetched_at,            │
                      │   source_timestamp,      │
                      │   measured_on, asset     │
                      │   CHECK(status!='OK'     │
                      │     OR measured_on=asset)│
                      └────────────┬─────────────┘
                                   │  polled, read-only
                                   ▼
                      ┌──────────────────────────┐
                      │  DASHBOARD (Vite/React)  │
                      │  Cloudflare Pages        │
                      │  behind Cloudflare Access│
                      │                          │
                      │  exhaustive switch on    │
                      │  status — UNAVAILABLE    │
                      │  renders "—", never "0"  │
                      └──────────────────────────┘
```

**The registry is the spine.** Adding an indicator is a row, never a migration (R0 §3b — the
prior schema was wide, one column pair per indicator, which is why integrity coverage was a
hand-maintained list that drifted). Integrity coverage is generated from the registry, so an
uncovered indicator is a build error rather than an oversight.

---

## Core schema decision

Long/narrow, provenance non-optional (R5 §2.2):

```sql
CREATE TYPE datapoint_status AS ENUM ('OK','STALE','UNAVAILABLE','ERROR');

CREATE TABLE datapoints (
  indicator_key   text  NOT NULL,
  asset           text  NOT NULL,   -- what we DISPLAY it as
  measured_on     text  NOT NULL,   -- what it was ACTUALLY computed on
  value           double precision, -- NULL unless OK/STALE
  status          datapoint_status NOT NULL,
  reason          text,             -- required for UNAVAILABLE/ERROR
  source_vendor   text  NOT NULL,
  endpoint        text  NOT NULL,   -- incl. the FIELD (F11)
  fetched_at      timestamptz NOT NULL,
  source_timestamp timestamptz,
  CONSTRAINT asset_match CHECK (status <> 'OK' OR measured_on = asset)
);
```

That CHECK constraint is the F2 defence: BTC's MVRV displayed as SOL's becomes a **database
error**, not a silent proxy. It is the single highest-leverage line in the schema.

`UNAVAILABLE` must further distinguish three reasons (R7 §C4) — `NOT_DEFINABLE` (SOPR on SOL:
account-based, no UTXO, not purchasable at any price), `PAYWALLED` (realized cap), and
`FETCH_FAILED`. One blank cell for all three destroys the information the owner most needs:
whether a gap is permanent, purchasable, or broken.

---

## Environments

| | Local | Preview | Production |
|---|---|---|---|
| URL | `localhost:5173` | `*.pages.dev` (per-branch) | Cloudflare Pages, behind Access |
| Database | Supabase project (same, read-only from app) | same | same |
| Secrets | `.env.local`, gitignored | Pages env vars | Pages env vars + GitHub Actions secrets |
| Ingestion | manual invoke | never scheduled | scheduled |

Single Supabase project. A second is not justified for one user, and divergence between two
databases is itself a silent-failure risk.

---

## Blast radius

Paths needing human review before merge (mirrored into `.uf/config.json`). Note these are
**product-specific** — there is no auth flow, no payments, no RLS surface of consequence:

- `**/registry*` — the indicator registry. Changing a definition retroactively changes the
  meaning of every stored value; this is the most dangerous file in the repo.
- `**/migrations/**` — schema, and especially the `asset_match` constraint.
- `**/fetchers/**` — endpoint or field changes silently alter what a number *is* (F11, F12).
- `.github/workflows/**` — the trigger layer; its silent failure cost 24h before.
- `**/status*`, `**/freshness*` — the fail-closed semantics themselves.

## Constraints

- **Budget: $0/mo for v1.** The paid-tier question reduces to a single row — SOL's on-chain
  column (R7 §C3). Everything else is genuinely free. Ship with SOL on-chain rendering
  `UNAVAILABLE — no free source`, which is a *truthful* display and precisely the product's
  purpose. Revisit only if the empty panel proves annoying in use.
- **GitHub Actions free minutes: 2,000/mo** (repo is private — verified). At ~3 min/run this
  allows ~22 runs/day. A 15-minute cadence would exceed it; cadence is a cost decision.
- **No secret may reach the browser.** The dashboard reads through the anon key against
  read-only views, or through Access-gated static JSON. No service-role key client-side, ever.
- **Determinism is a hard requirement**, not a nicety: indicator computation is a pure
  function of (bars, window), golden-file pinned. The prior system's values depended on
  process uptime (R0/F5).
- **Vendor churn is assumed, not exceptional.** Four sources broke or gated in nine months
  (R0 §3); CryptoCompare retired its free tier entirely in May 2026 and pytrends is archived
  (R4). Every fetcher is cassette-tested so a silent response-shape change fails loudly.

# Mobile & PWA

> Mobile & PWA is the layer that extends a web product onto phones and tablets, either by making your existing site installable and offline-capable (a Progressive Web App) or by shipping a real app to the Apple App Store and Google Play built from a shared codebase (React Native, Expo, Flutter, Capacitor, etc.). The strategic question is rarely "web or native" but *how much* native you need: a responsive site covers most reach for free, a PWA adds installability/offline/limited push, and a cross-platform framework buys you store presence, deep device APIs, and richer push, at the cost of store fees, review cycles, and a build/release pipeline. The cheapest path that meets your requirements wins.

This document is technology-agnostic. Choose based on required device capabilities, distribution channel (store vs. URL), team skillset (web vs. native), and budget. **All prices are USD and current as of June 2026; verify on vendor pricing pages before committing, as this market re-prices frequently.** Apple Developer Program is **$99/yr**; Google Play Developer is a **$25 one-time** fee.

Think of it as a ladder of increasing capability and cost:

# Testing & QA

> Testing & QA is the safety net that proves software actually works before users (or auditors) find out it doesn't. It spans a pyramid: many fast **unit tests** (single functions/components), fewer **integration tests** (modules + real dependencies), and a thin top of **end-to-end (E2E)** tests (full browser/user flows), wrapped by **component/visual regression**, **load/performance**, **API/contract**, and **accessibility** testing. In the age of AI, this layer is *more* important, not less: AI build agents and copilots generate plausible-looking code fast, but plausible is not correct. Tests are the executable specification that catches hallucinated APIs, off-by-one logic, broken edge cases, and regressions an LLM happily introduces while "fixing" something else. The modern playbook for an AI agent: write tests alongside the code, run them in CI on every change, gate merges/deploys on green (cross-ref `13-cicd-and-devops`), and lean on AI for the tedious parts (generating test scaffolds, Playwright codegen, self-healing selectors) while keeping a human-reviewable assertion of *intended behavior*. Free/OSS runners (Vitest, pytest, Playwright) cover ~90% of needs; you only pay for cloud device grids, visual-diff SaaS, and managed load generation when scale or browser/device coverage demands it.

# Split cadence — daily collect, fast derivatives, and the 6h canary

## What this delivers

The single `ingest` workflow, which currently collects every registered indicator on one
uniform 6-hourly cron regardless of that indicator's own real update cadence, splits into three
cadence tiers sharing one Python entrypoint: a **fast** tier (12 entries: OKX open interest,
long/short ratio, taker ratio — all on 300s freshness bounds) triggered externally by
cron-job.org every 5 minutes via `repository_dispatch`, a **medium** tier (4 entries: OKX funding
rate, 28800s bounds) on native GitHub Actions schedule, and the existing **daily** tier (54
entries: technical indicators, Coin Metrics, Validators.app staking, 86400s bounds), also on
native schedule. The already-existing `contract-canary` workflow (built in US-206, 6-hourly,
writes nothing) is confirmed unchanged. Separately, `sol_active_addresses`'s registry entry gets
its declared freshness fields corrected to match its real weekly schedule (set in PRD-007), fixing
a live mismatch discovered during this PRD's own G1 verification, not something this PRD's
cadence-split logic itself introduces or depends on.

## Why (from research and this gate's own findings)

Three findings are load-bearing.

1. **The brief's own stated risk was wrong; the real risk already caused a production incident
   in this codebase.** The brief worried that splitting collection across separate CI runner IPs
   would multiply vendor rate-limit exposure. Research found this premise false — GitHub-hosted
   runners already get a fresh IP per job run today, for the single combined job, so splitting
   changes nothing about IP diversity. The real risk research surfaced instead is a repeat of
   PRD-007's Helius incident: a tightened cadence's wall-clock budget colliding with the
   scheduler's own timeout, which nobody had checked for the *new* fast-tier job specifically.
2. **GitHub Actions cron cannot hold a 5-minute cadence against a 450-second freshness bound.**
   GitHub's own docs confirm scheduled runs are delayed under load, clustering "at the start of
   every hour"; independent measurement found ~1-in-10 runs land 5+ minutes late and ~1-in-50
   land 15+ minutes late, with community reports of 60+ minute peak delays. The fast tier's own
   `freshness_stale_seconds: 600` cannot absorb that without frequent false-STALE reads
   indistinguishable from a real vendor outage. cron-job.org, already an adopted trigger pattern
   in this project's architecture doc, documents 4-40 second dispatch delay — two orders of
   magnitude tighter — but was never actually provisioned (`15_Services_and_Credentials.md` marks
   it "N/A until PRD-012" verbatim).
3. **`sol_active_addresses` already has a live cadence-vs-contract mismatch, discovered during
   this gate, not anticipated by the brief.** Its registry entry declares `86400`/`172800`
   (daily/2-day) freshness fields, but its real dedicated schedule
   (`sol-active-addresses.yml`, built in PRD-007's US-707 for Helius's credit budget) only runs
   weekly. The cell currently reads `STALE` against its own declared contract for roughly 5 of
   every 7 days. This PRD corrects the declared fields to match the real schedule — it does not
   change the schedule itself, which is a separate, already-settled owner decision.

## Approach

**One shared entrypoint, filtered by tier.** `ingest/pipeline.py`'s existing `run_all_assets`/
`run_pipeline`/`run_scheduled_board` machinery already reads every registered indicator from
`ingest/registry.yaml`; this PRD adds a `--tier {fast,medium,daily}` filter (or equivalent
programmatic parameter) that restricts a run to only the registry rows whose
`expected_update_interval_seconds` matches that tier's own value (`300` for fast, `28800` for
medium, `86400` for daily — no new registry field, the discriminator already exists). No
fetch/write/heartbeat logic is duplicated across tiers; a fix to shared pipeline logic needs one
change, not three.

**Three workflow files, one shared script.** `ingest-fast.yml` drops `schedule:` entirely and
triggers only on `repository_dispatch` (type `ingest-fast`) plus `workflow_dispatch` as a manual
fallback, matching the naming convention already used by `canary`/`ingest`/`sol-active-addresses`.
`ingest-medium.yml` keeps a native `schedule:` cron (8-hourly, offset away from `:00`/`:05` per
GitHub's own recommendation and the existing `ingest.yml`'s own `17 */6 * * *` precedent).
`ingest.yml` itself is renamed/repurposed as the daily tier, keeping its existing offset cron
but moved to once-daily instead of every 6 hours. Each gets its own dedicated Healthchecks.io
check and Grace Time, following the vendor's own documented "one check per job" practice — well
within the 20-check free tier alongside the existing `HEALTHCHECK_URL_CONTRACT_CANARY` and
`sol-active-addresses` checks.

**cron-job.org fires the fast tier's `repository_dispatch` every 5 minutes**, using a
fine-grained PAT scoped to this repo's Actions read/write (`GH_DISPATCH_PAT`, per
`15_Services_and_Credentials.md`'s own documented shape) — provisioned as part of this PRD, not
assumed to already exist. A real timed dry run of the fast tier's full wall-clock budget
(checkout + `uv` install + 12 OKX calls + writes + heartbeat) happens before this criterion is
accepted, not estimated on paper, per the assumption above.

**`sol_active_addresses`'s freshness fields are corrected** to values that actually fit a weekly
schedule (e.g. `expected_update_interval_seconds` reflecting the real ~7-day cadence, with
`freshness_warn_seconds`/`freshness_stale_seconds` sized with real headroom above that, not the
current daily/2-day values) — a small, isolated registry change, verified by confirming the cell
no longer reads `STALE` immediately after a normal weekly run completes.

## Data model changes

None. This PRD changes *when* existing registered indicators are collected and corrects one
entry's declared freshness fields to match an already-existing schedule; it adds no new column,
migration, indicator, or vendor.

## Out of scope

Restated from `00-brief.md`, confirmed at G1: rebuilding the contract-canary workflow (already
exists, unchanged); changing `sol-active-addresses.yml`'s own weekly schedule (only its
registry-declared freshness fields are corrected here); any new indicator, vendor, or panel; any
composite freshness score or health dashboard (PRD-010); resolving whether continuous 5-minute
automated polling violates OKX's usage-pattern terms beyond the numeric rate limit (flagged
`UNVERIFIED` by research at the primary-source level — the fast tier's acceptance criteria must
not assume this is settled).

## The adversarial case

**Force a fast-tier cell (e.g. `btc_open_interest`) stale by simulating a missed collection
window, and confirm it reads `STALE` within its existing 450-second freshness-warn bound — not
hours or days later** because a coarser tier silently absorbed it. **A second case, directly
guarding against the blind spot research flagged**: confirm the daily tier's own `--tier` filter
does not silently drop a row that belongs to it — i.e., that the union of fast + medium + daily
tier runs, over one full cycle, writes exactly the same 71-row set the single combined job used
to write, with no row falling through a filter gap or landing in the wrong tier. A third,
cheaper case: confirm `contract-canary`'s own 6-hourly heartbeat still fires correctly once the
main collect workflow's shape changes, proving the two schedules are genuinely independent, not
accidentally coupled through a shared trigger, secret, or credential rate limit.

## Stories

| Story | Title | Depends on |
|---|---|---|
| US-1201 | Registry tier filter — one shared entrypoint accepts `--tier {fast,medium,daily}`, partitioning by `expected_update_interval_seconds` with no row dropped or duplicated | — |

# CI/CD & DevOps

> CI/CD and DevOps are the machinery that turns code into running software safely and repeatably. **CI (continuous integration)** runs tests, linting, and builds on every change; **CD (continuous delivery/deployment)** promotes artifacts through environments to production. For an AI building agent: keep pipelines in the same platform as the code when possible (GitHub repo → GitHub Actions), define infrastructure as code from day one, ship in containers for portability, and use feature flags to decouple deploy from release. # Split cadence — daily collect, fast derivatives, and the 6h canary

## What this delivers

The single `ingest` workflow, which currently collects every registered indicator on one
uniform 6-hourly cron regardless of that indicator's own real update cadence, splits into three
cadence tiers sharing one Python entrypoint: a **fast** tier (12 entries: OKX open interest,
long/short ratio, taker ratio — all on 300s freshness bounds) triggered externally by
cron-job.org every 5 minutes via `repository_dispatch`, a **medium** tier (4 entries: OKX funding
rate, 28800s bounds) on native GitHub Actions schedule, and the existing **daily** tier (54
entries: technical indicators, Coin Metrics, Validators.app staking, 86400s bounds), also on
native schedule. The already-existing `contract-canary` workflow (built in US-206, 6-hourly,
writes nothing) is confirmed unchanged. Separately, `sol_active_addresses`'s registry entry gets
its declared freshness fields corrected to match its real weekly schedule (set in PRD-007), fixing
a live mismatch discovered during this PRD's own G1 verification, not something this PRD's
cadence-split logic itself introduces or depends on.

## Why (from research and this gate's own findings)

Three findings are load-bearing.

1. **The brief's own stated risk was wrong; the real risk already caused a production incident
   in this codebase.** The brief worried that splitting collection across separate CI runner IPs
   would multiply vendor rate-limit exposure. Research found this premise false — GitHub-hosted
   runners already get a fresh IP per job run today, for the single combined job, so splitting
   changes nothing about IP diversity. The real risk research surfaced instead is a repeat of
   PRD-007's Helius incident: a tightened cadence's wall-clock budget colliding with the
   scheduler's own timeout, which nobody had checked for the *new* fast-tier job specifically.
2. **GitHub Actions cron cannot hold a 5-minute cadence against a 450-second freshness bound.**
   GitHub's own docs confirm scheduled runs are delayed under load, clustering "at the start of
   every hour"; independent measurement found ~1-in-10 runs land 5+ minutes late and ~1-in-50
   land 15+ minutes late, with community reports of 60+ minute peak delays. The fast tier's own
   `freshness_stale_seconds: 600` cannot absorb that without frequent false-STALE reads
   indistinguishable from a real vendor outage. cron-job.org, already an adopted trigger pattern
   in this project's architecture doc, documents 4-40 second dispatch delay — two orders of
   magnitude tighter — but was never actually provisioned (`15_Services_and_Credentials.md` marks
   it "N/A until PRD-012" verbatim).
3. **`sol_active_addresses` already has a live cadence-vs-contract mismatch, discovered during
   this gate, not anticipated by the brief.** Its registry entry declares `86400`/`172800`
   (daily/2-day) freshness fields, but its real dedicated schedule
   (`sol-active-addresses.yml`, built in PRD-007's US-707 for Helius's credit budget) only runs
   weekly. The cell currently reads `STALE` against its own declared contract for roughly 5 of
   every 7 days. This PRD corrects the declared fields to match the real schedule — it does not
   change the schedule itself, which is a separate, already-settled owner decision.

## Approach

**One shared entrypoint, filtered by tier.** `ingest/pipeline.py`'s existing `run_all_assets`/
`run_pipeline`/`run_scheduled_board` machinery already reads every registered indicator from
`ingest/registry.yaml`; this PRD adds a `--tier {fast,medium,daily}` filter (or equivalent
programmatic parameter) that restricts a run to only the registry rows whose
`expected_update_interval_seconds` matches that tier's own value (`300` for fast, `28800` for
medium, `86400` for daily — no new registry field, the discriminator already exists). No
fetch/write/heartbeat logic is duplicated across tiers; a fix to shared pipeline logic needs one
change, not three.

**Three workflow files, one shared script.** `ingest-fast.yml` drops `schedule:` entirely and
triggers only on `repository_dispatch` (type `ingest-fast`) plus `workflow_dispatch` as a manual
fallback, matching the naming convention already used by `canary`/`ingest`/`sol-active-addresses`.
`ingest-medium.yml` keeps a native `schedule:` cron (8-hourly, offset away from `:00`/`:05` per
GitHub's own recommendation and the existing `ingest.yml`'s own `17 */6 * * *` precedent).
`ingest.yml` itself is renamed/repurposed as the daily tier, keeping its existing offset cron
but moved to once-daily instead of every 6 hours. Each gets its own dedicated Healthchecks.io
check and Grace Time, following the vendor's own documented "one check per job" practice — well
within the 20-check free tier alongside the existing `HEALTHCHECK_URL_CONTRACT_CANARY` and
`sol-active-addresses` checks.

**cron-job.org fires the fast tier's `repository_dispatch` every 5 minutes**, using a
fine-grained PAT scoped to this repo's Actions read/write (`GH_DISPATCH_PAT`, per
`15_Services_and_Credentials.md`'s own documented shape) — provisioned as part of this PRD, not
assumed to already exist. A real timed dry run of the fast tier's full wall-clock budget
(checkout + `uv` install + 12 OKX calls + writes + heartbeat) happens before this criterion is
accepted, not estimated on paper, per the assumption above.

**`sol_active_addresses`'s freshness fields are corrected** to values that actually fit a weekly
schedule (e.g. `expected_update_interval_seconds` reflecting the real ~7-day cadence, with
`freshness_warn_seconds`/`freshness_stale_seconds` sized with real headroom above that, not the
current daily/2-day values) — a small, isolated registry change, verified by confirming the cell
no longer reads `STALE` immediately after a normal weekly run completes.

## Data model changes

None. This PRD changes *when* existing registered indicators are collected and corrects one
entry's declared freshness fields to match an already-existing schedule; it adds no new column,
migration, indicator, or vendor.

## Out of scope

Restated from `00-brief.md`, confirmed at G1: rebuilding the contract-canary workflow (already
exists, unchanged); changing `sol-active-addresses.yml`'s own weekly schedule (only its
registry-declared freshness fields are corrected here); any new indicator, vendor, or panel; any
composite freshness score or health dashboard (PRD-010); resolving whether continuous 5-minute
automated polling violates OKX's usage-pattern terms beyond the numeric rate limit (flagged
`UNVERIFIED` by research at the primary-source level — the fast tier's acceptance criteria must
not assume this is settled).

## The adversarial case

**Force a fast-tier cell (e.g. `btc_open_interest`) stale by simulating a missed collection
window, and confirm it reads `STALE` within its existing 450-second freshness-warn bound — not
hours or days later** because a coarser tier silently absorbed it. **A second case, directly
guarding against the blind spot research flagged**: confirm the daily tier's own `--tier` filter
does not silently drop a row that belongs to it — i.e., that the union of fast + medium + daily
tier runs, over one full cycle, writes exactly the same 71-row set the single combined job used
to write, with no row falling through a filter gap or landing in the wrong tier. A third,
cheaper case: confirm `contract-canary`'s own 6-hourly heartbeat still fires correctly once the
main collect workflow's shape changes, proving the two schedules are genuinely independent, not
accidentally coupled through a shared trigger, secret, or credential rate limit.

# CI/CD & DevOps

> CI/CD and DevOps are the machinery that turns code into running software safely and repeatably. **CI (continuous integration)** runs tests, linting, and builds on every change; **CD (continuous delivery/deployment)** promotes artifacts through environments to production. Around that core sit four supporting disciplines: **version control & collaboration** (GitHub/GitLab/Bitbucket - where code lives and PRs/reviews happen), **IaC (infrastructure as code)** (Terraform/OpenTofu/Pulumi - provision cloud resources declaratively), **containers & registries** (Docker images + GHCR/Docker Hub + orchestration), and **environment/release management** (dev/staging/prod separation, feature flags, progressive delivery). For an AI building agent: keep pipelines in the same platform as the code when possible (GitHub repo → GitHub Actions), define infrastructure as code from day one, ship in containers for portability, and use feature flags to decouple deploy from release. The recurring cost trap is CI minutes - especially **macOS runners (~10x Linux)** and missing caches.

# PRD-012 · Split cadence — research

## What we already knew, and whether it still holds

| Claim from our knowledge base | Still true? | What the source says | Citation |
|---|---|---|---|
| GitHub Actions `schedule:` runners are the compute layer (owner decision 2026-09-08, measured reachability) | **Holds** | Not contradicted by anything found. Reachability was measured for spot/derivatives/on-chain venues, not a cadence question. | (internal, `10-architecture.md`) |
| "GH Actions cron is documented to delay and occasionally drop runs" (already flagged as residual risk in the architecture doc) | **Holds, and is worse than the architecture doc implies for sub-hourly cadence** | GitHub's own docs: "The `schedule` event can be delayed during periods of high loads... High load times include the start of every hour... some queued jobs may be dropped." Independent measurement: "About 1 in 10 lands 5+ minutes late. About 1 in 50 lands 15+ minutes late," with community reports of 60+ minute delays at peak. | https://docs.github.com/en/actions/using-workflows/events-that-trigger-workflows#schedule , https://crontap.com/blog/github-actions-cron-drift-problem |
| "cron-job.org, already used elsewhere in this project's stack" as a fallback trigger mechanism | **Holds as a viable alternative, needs one correction** | cron-job.org supports down to 1-minute intervals on the free plan ("no rate limiting on 1-minute intervals") but is explicit that punctuality is *not guaranteed*: "delay time before running cronjobs ranging from 4 to 40 seconds." It is a better floor than GH Actions' 5-minute minimum + peak-hour drift, but it is not a hard real-time guarantee either — the freshness bound still needs slack for this. | https://cron-job.org/en/faq/ |
| Healthchecks.io free tier (20 checks) is "the single highest value-per-effort defence" | **Holds, and directly supports a per-tier design** | Healthchecks.io's own docs recommend one check per monitored job ("you would create a separate check for each cron job to be monitored") with a Grace Time set "a little above the expected duration of your cron job" — i.e. the product already has headroom (contract-canary uses one dedicated check today; PRD-012 would add at most 1–2 more, well inside the 20-check free tier). | https://healthchecks.io/docs/configuring_checks/ |
| "each job is a separate CI runner with a separate IP" (brief's stated risk about splitting collection multiplying vendor rate-limit exposure) | **Partially wrong — the premise doesn't hold on GitHub-hosted runners** | GitHub-hosted runners are ephemeral VMs with pool egress; "each job is an ephemeral VM... you'll almost certainly see two different addresses" even for *runs of the same workflow*. This is already true today for the single `ingest` job — every run already gets a fresh IP within Azure/Azure US ranges. Splitting into fast/medium/daily jobs does not introduce a *new* multi-IP exposure; that exposure already exists per-run. What splitting *does* change is call-volume clustering in time, not apparent source diversity. | https://docs.ipconfig.io/guides/github-actions-runner-ip , https://github.com/orgs/community/discussions/26884 |
| "The existing `contract-canary` workflow... does not need to be rebuilt" | Not independently web-verifiable (internal artifact) — confirmed by reading `.github/workflows/canary.yml` directly rather than the web; no correction needed here. | — | (file read, not web) |

## Existing implementations

No public reference implementation matches this exact shape (multi-tier crypto-indicator collection split across GitHub Actions cron tiers with a separate contract-canary heartbeat), but the individual pieces are each well-trodden:

- **GitHub Actions as a scheduler for data pipelines** is a widely-documented pattern, but every serious writeup converges on the same caveat this PRD must design around: treat `schedule:` "as a trigger source, not the clock" for anything time-sensitive, and prefer running the real clock in an external scheduler (cron-job.org, EventBridge, etc.) that fires `workflow_dispatch`/`repository_dispatch` — GitHub Actions supplies compute, not punctuality. https://crontap.com/blog/github-actions-cron-drift-problem
- **cron-job.org + `repository_dispatch`** is exactly the pattern this repo's own architecture doc already committed to as the "independent second trigger" for `ingest` — this PRD's fast tier is a natural extension of an already-adopted pattern, not a new integration.
- **Healthchecks.io "one check per job" with per-check Grace Time** is the vendor's own documented best practice for exactly this problem (multiple independently-scheduled jobs each needing their own dead-man's-switch): https://healthchecks.io/docs/configuring_checks/

## Approach options

**Option A — Three separate GitHub Actions workflows (fast/medium/daily), each with its own `cron:` and its own `HEALTHCHECKS_PING_URL_*`**
How it works: split `ingest.yml` into `ingest-fast.yml` (`*/5 * * * *`, the 12 five-minute OKX rows), `ingest-medium.yml` (8-hour cron, the 4 funding-rate rows), and `ingest-daily.yml` (renamed current job, the 54 daily rows). Each filters the registry by its own tier at runtime (`expected_update_interval_seconds` already exists as the discriminator — no new registry field needed).
Trade-offs: Simplest to reason about; reuses the exact `expected_update_interval_seconds` field the registry already carries. But the fast tier inherits GitHub's documented 5-minute-minimum + peak-hour drift risk (https://docs.github.com/en/actions/using-workflows/events-that-trigger-workflows#schedule) — a run landing 15 minutes late against a 600s freshness-warn bound (`btc_open_interest` etc.) means the cell reads `WARN`/`STALE` through no fault of the vendor or the code, purely GH Actions queue congestion at top-of-hour.
Cost: $0 (same GH Actions free-tier minutes budget, just redistributed across three workflows instead of one — total call volume is unchanged, only its clustering).
Who uses it: This is the "just use GH Actions schedule directly" default seen across most GH-Actions-as-cron writeups; it's the cheapest to build and matches what `sol-active-addresses.yml` already precedent-sets (dedicated workflow per tier).

**Option B — Same three-tier split, but the fast tier is triggered by cron-job.org → `repository_dispatch` instead of native GH Actions `schedule:`**
How it works: identical job bodies to Option A, but `ingest-fast.yml` drops its `schedule:` trigger entirely and listens only for `repository_dispatch` (type e.g. `ingest-fast`); a cron-job.org job fires that dispatch every 5 minutes.
Trade-offs: Removes GH Actions' documented top-of-hour congestion risk for the tier that actually can't absorb a 15-minute miss (600s/450s freshness bounds). Costs one more moving part (a cron-job.org job to configure and monitor) but the project's architecture doc already adopted cron-job.org as the fallback trigger for exactly this reason. cron-job.org itself is not zero-drift either (4–40s dispatch delay, https://cron-job.org/en/faq/) but that is two orders of magnitude tighter than GH Actions' reported 5–30+ minute peak drift.
Cost: $0 (cron-job.org free tier).
Who uses it: This is precisely the pattern the crontap writeup recommends for any schedule tighter than hourly (https://crontap.com/blog/github-actions-cron-drift-problem), and matches this project's own architecture-doc precedent of cron-job.org as "an independent second trigger."

**Option C — Keep one combined job, add a `--tier` flag, and just tighten the single cron to run more often**
How it works: don't split workflows; instead call the existing `ingest` entrypoint every 5 minutes but have it internally skip any indicator whose `expected_update_interval_seconds` hasn't elapsed since its last write (idempotent no-op for daily/medium rows most runs).
Trade-offs: Avoids multiplying workflow files, but every run — even the ~283 out of 288 daily runs per day that do nothing — still pays the fixed CI overhead (checkout, `uv` setup, DB connection) for zero benefit, and a single job now has to reason about mixed timeout budgets (the fast tier's OKX calls plus a daily row's occasional TA-Lib recompute in the same process). This directly risks recreating the known "a live fetch that fits its API budget can still break a scheduled job on wall-clock time alone" failure mode already logged against this exact codebase — a slow daily-tier fetch inside a job now running every 5 minutes shrinks the effective timeout budget for the fast tier sharing that same run.
Cost: $0, but wastes the most GH Actions minutes of the three options (288 daily invocations vs. Option A/B's daily job running once).
Who uses it: Not found in any external writeup for exactly this reason — the "one flexible cron, skip internally" pattern is a known anti-pattern once tiers diverge by more than ~10x in frequency, which this registry's 300s vs 86400s split (288x) clearly does.

**Recommendation: Option B.** The 5-minute tier's own freshness contract (450s stale bound) cannot absorb GH Actions' own documented delay behavior at that cadence, and the project has already adopted cron-job.org as a trigger mechanism for exactly this reason — Option B is a small, already-precedented extension, not new infrastructure. The 8-hour and daily tiers can stay on native GH Actions `schedule:` (Option A) since a 15–30 minute drift is immaterial against a 43200s/108000s freshness bound.

## Edge cases and gotchas

- **The wall-clock-vs-rate-limit distinction already bit this exact codebase once** (Helius/Solana fetch measured against credit budget but not against the CI job's own 10-minute timeout, taking 2.5h against a 10-minute limit). The current `ingest.yml` has `timeout-minutes: 10` (confirmed by reading the file). Splitting into a 5-minute-cadence fast-tier job means that job's *own* wall-clock budget must be far under 5 minutes end-to-end (checkout + `uv` install + 12 OKX calls + writes), or successive scheduled runs will start overlapping/queueing — verify this with a real timed run, not an estimate, exactly as the prior incident's fix note prescribes.
- **OKX's public market-data rate limit is per-IP, not per-account**, and open-interest specifically is rate-limited at roughly 20 requests per 2 seconds (community-sourced, OKX's own per-endpoint doc page did not resolve the number directly on fetch — flagging this as **UNVERIFIED at the primary-source level**, sourced instead from a secondary aggregator). At 12 five-minute-tier rows × one call each, this PRD's fast tier is nowhere near that ceiling even before considering that GitHub-hosted runner IPs are already ephemeral per-run (see table above) — so the brief's stated worry about "multiplying rate limits across separate runner IPs" does not hold on the numbers found; the real constraint is wall-clock timeout, not rate limit.
- **GH Actions top-of-hour congestion is not evenly distributed** — delays cluster specifically "at the start of every hour" per GitHub's own docs. A fast-tier cron of `*/5 * * * *` hits every hour-boundary by construction, so if the medium/daily tiers are *also* scheduled near `:00`, all three tiers' worst-case-drift moments coincide. Stagger daily/medium cron minutes away from `:00`/`:05` (GitHub's own recommendation: "schedule your workflow to run at a different time of the hour," https://docs.github.com/en/actions/using-workflows/events-that-trigger-workflows#schedule) — the existing `ingest.yml` already does this (`cron: '17 */6 * * *'`, offset 17 minutes), so this practice just needs to be preserved, not newly invented, when the workflow is split.
- **A public repo's scheduled workflow auto-disables after 60 days of no repository activity** (GitHub's own docs, confirmed above) — worth noting for whichever new workflow file is least likely to see commits touching it, though this repo is presumably private and this is likely moot; **UNVERIFIED** whether the repo is public or private from research alone.

## Services and keys this PRD needs

| Service | Why | Env var | Already provisioned? |
|---|---|---|---|
| cron-job.org | External trigger for the 5-minute fast tier, if Option B is chosen, to avoid GH Actions' documented schedule drift at sub-hourly cadence | none (webhook target is a GitHub `repository_dispatch` endpoint using a PAT) | Likely yes — architecture doc states cron-job.org is "already used elsewhere in this project's stack"; confirm which existing workflow uses it and reuse its dispatch token rather than minting a new one |
| Healthchecks.io | One additional check + Grace Time for the fast-tier job's own heartbeat, separate from `HEALTHCHECK_URL_CONTRACT_CANARY` and the existing daily-ingest heartbeat | e.g. `HEALTHCHECK_URL_INGEST_FAST` | Not yet — new check needed, but well within the 20-check free tier |

## Open questions for the human

# Split cadence — daily collect, fast derivatives, and the 6h canary

## What this delivers

The single `ingest` workflow, which currently collects every registered indicator on one
uniform 6-hourly cron regardless of that indicator's own real update cadence, splits into three
cadence tiers sharing one Python entrypoint: a **fast** tier (12 entries: OKX open interest,
long/short ratio, taker ratio — all on 300s freshness bounds) triggered externally by
cron-job.org every 5 minutes via `repository_dispatch`, a **medium** tier (4 entries: OKX funding
rate, 28800s bounds) on native GitHub Actions schedule, and the existing **daily** tier (54
entries: technical indicators, Coin Metrics, Validators.app staking, 86400s bounds), also on
native schedule. The already-existing `contract-canary` workflow (built in US-206, 6-hourly,
writes nothing) is confirmed unchanged. Separately, `sol_active_addresses`'s registry entry gets
its declared freshness fields corrected to match its real weekly schedule (set in PRD-007), fixing
a live mismatch discovered during this PRD's own G1 verification, not something this PRD's
cadence-split logic itself introduces or depends on.

## Why (from research and this gate's own findings)

Three findings are load-bearing.

1. **The brief's own stated risk was wrong; the real risk already caused a production incident
   in this codebase.** The brief worried that splitting collection across separate CI runner IPs
   would multiply vendor rate-limit exposure. Research found this premise false — GitHub-hosted
   runners already get a fresh IP per job run today, for the single combined job, so splitting
   changes nothing about IP diversity. The real risk research surfaced instead is a repeat of
   PRD-007's Helius incident: a tightened cadence's wall-clock budget colliding with the
   scheduler's own timeout, which nobody had checked for the *new* fast-tier job specifically.
2. **GitHub Actions cron cannot hold a 5-minute cadence against a 450-second freshness bound.**
   GitHub's own docs confirm scheduled runs are delayed under load, clustering "at the start of
   every hour"; independent measurement found ~1-in-10 runs land 5+ minutes late and ~1-in-50
   land 15+ minutes late, with community reports of 60+ minute peak delays. The fast tier's own
   `freshness_stale_seconds: 600` cannot absorb that without frequent false-STALE reads
   indistinguishable from a real vendor outage. cron-job.org, already an adopted trigger pattern
   in this project's architecture doc, documents 4-40 second dispatch delay — two orders of
   magnitude tighter — but was never actually provisioned (`15_Services_and_Credentials.md` marks
   it "N/A until PRD-012" verbatim).
3. **`sol_active_addresses` already has a live cadence-vs-contract mismatch, discovered during
   this gate, not anticipated by the brief.** Its registry entry declares `86400`/`172800`
   (daily/2-day) freshness fields, but its real dedicated schedule
   (`sol-active-addresses.yml`, built in PRD-007's US-707 for Helius's credit budget) only runs
   weekly. The cell currently reads `STALE` against its own declared contract for roughly 5 of
   every 7 days. This PRD corrects the declared fields to match the real schedule — it does not
   change the schedule itself, which is a separate, already-settled owner decision.

## Approach

**One shared entrypoint, filtered by tier.** `ingest/pipeline.py`'s existing `run_all_assets`/
`run_pipeline`/`run_scheduled_board` machinery already reads every registered indicator from
`ingest/registry.yaml`; this PRD adds a `--tier {fast,medium,daily}` filter (or equivalent
programmatic parameter) that restricts a run to only the registry rows whose
`expected_update_interval_seconds` matches that tier's own value (`300` for fast, `28800` for
medium, `86400` for daily — no new registry field, the discriminator already exists). No
fetch/write/heartbeat logic is duplicated across tiers; a fix to shared pipeline logic needs one
change, not three.

**Three workflow files, one shared script.** `ingest-fast.yml` drops `schedule:` entirely and
triggers only on `repository_dispatch` (type `ingest-fast`) plus `workflow_dispatch` as a manual
fallback, matching the naming convention already used by `canary`/`ingest`/`sol-active-addresses`.
`ingest-medium.yml` keeps a native `schedule:` cron (8-hourly, offset away from `:00`/`:05` per
GitHub's own recommendation and the existing `ingest.yml`'s own `17 */6 * * *` precedent).
`ingest.yml` itself is renamed/repurposed as the daily tier, keeping its existing offset cron
but moved to once-daily instead of every 6 hours. Each gets its own dedicated Healthchecks.io
check and Grace Time, following the vendor's own documented "one check per job" practice — well
within the 20-check free tier alongside the existing `HEALTHCHECK_URL_CONTRACT_CANARY` and
`sol-active-addresses` checks.

**cron-job.org fires the fast tier's `repository_dispatch` every 5 minutes**, using a
fine-grained PAT scoped to this repo's Actions read/write (`GH_DISPATCH_PAT`, per
`15_Services_and_Credentials.md`'s own documented shape) — provisioned as part of this PRD, not
assumed to already exist. A real timed dry run of the fast tier's full wall-clock budget
(checkout + `uv` install + 12 OKX calls + writes + heartbeat) happens before this criterion is
accepted, not estimated on paper, per the assumption above.

**`sol_active_addresses`'s freshness fields are corrected** to values that actually fit a weekly
schedule (e.g. `expected_update_interval_seconds` reflecting the real ~7-day cadence, with
`freshness_warn_seconds`/`freshness_stale_seconds` sized with real headroom above that, not the
current daily/2-day values) — a small, isolated registry change, verified by confirming the cell
no longer reads `STALE` immediately after a normal weekly run completes.

## Data model changes

None. This PRD changes *when* existing registered indicators are collected and corrects one
entry's declared freshness fields to match an already-existing schedule; it adds no new column,
migration, indicator, or vendor.

## Out of scope

Restated from `00-brief.md`, confirmed at G1: rebuilding the contract-canary workflow (already
exists, unchanged); changing `sol-active-addresses.yml`'s own weekly schedule (only its
registry-declared freshness fields are corrected here); any new indicator, vendor, or panel; any
composite freshness score or health dashboard (PRD-010); resolving whether continuous 5-minute
automated polling violates OKX's usage-pattern terms beyond the numeric rate limit (flagged
`UNVERIFIED` by research at the primary-source level — the fast tier's acceptance criteria must
not assume this is settled).

## The adversarial case

**Force a fast-tier cell (e.g. `btc_open_interest`) stale by simulating a missed collection
window, and confirm it reads `STALE` within its existing 450-second freshness-warn bound — not
hours or days later** because a coarser tier silently absorbed it. **A second case, directly
guarding against the blind spot research flagged**: confirm the daily tier's own `--tier` filter
does not silently drop a row that belongs to it — i.e., that the union of fast + medium + daily
tier runs, over one full cycle, writes exactly the same 71-row set the single combined job used
to write, with no row falling through a filter gap or landing in the wrong tier. A third,
cheaper case: confirm `contract-canary`'s own 6-hourly heartbeat still fires correctly once the
main collect workflow's shape changes, proving the two schedules are genuinely independent, not
accidentally coupled through a shared trigger, secret, or credential rate limit.

> Testing & QA is the safety net that proves software actually works before users (or auditors) find out it doesn't. In the age of AI, this layer is *more* important, not less: AI build agents and copilots generate plausible-looking code fast, but plausible is not correct. Tests are the executable specification that catches hallucinated APIs, off-by-one logic, broken edge cases, and regressions an LLM happily introduces while "fixing" something else.
